clips.why: A short, focused demo of the bug in this lesson and the env: fix, by an experienced maintainer.
look: What the shell receives once GitHub has filled in the expression.
A value that changes the script after it is pasted in.
His tip for keeping the value out of the script text; compare it with env: in this lesson.

clips.title: Lessons From a CI/CD Supply Chain Attack at Grafana Labs
clips.why: Grafana's security team tells how a real attacker got into their CI through a risky workflow trigger.
look: Why pull_request_target was the opening: it runs with the base repo's secrets on events from strangers.
How the attacker used a pull request to reach that workflow.
How little the attacker needed: one misconfigured trigger.
clips.after: The same family of risk is why zizmor flags workflow_run, and why our trigger workflow never checks out PR code and holds no secrets.

clips.title: Securely deploy to AWS with GitHub Actions and OIDC
clips.why: GitHub's own one-minute explanation of what OIDC is, before the setup details.
look: The job gets a short-lived token instead of a stored key.
The cloud provider trusts GitHub's signature and checks who the job is.
Why there is nothing long-lived left to leak.
clips.after: fcp's integration tests and our routine trigger use this: id-token: write, a signed token, and credentials that last minutes.

practice.q: Which of these event fields can carry an attack into a run: step?

options.why: GitHub sets it, and it is always a number.
Anyone who opens a PR chooses the branch name, and git allows characters like $( ) in it.
It is the repo's own owner/name, set by GitHub, not by the person who opened the PR.

practice.q: Finish the safe version: the title arrives as an environment variable.
practice.hint: Read the variable, in double quotes so that spaces stay part of the value.
practice.why: "$TITLE" passes the title to printf as one value. bash never parses the contents of a variable as code.

practice.q: In actions/github-script, finish the line that reads the PR title safely.
practice.hint: The object that holds the event, plus the field that holds its JSON.
practice.why: context.payload is the event as a JavaScript object, so the title is a string in a variable, never part of the source.

practice.q: Put what happens to a run: step with an expression in order.
items: A person writes a PR title, and a workflow is triggered
GitHub evaluates each ${{ }} and pastes the result into the script text
The runner saves the script and starts bash on it
bash parses the text, including whatever the title contained, and runs it
practice.why: The pasting happens before bash starts, so bash cannot tell your code from the title. env: moves the title out of the text and into a variable.

practice.q: A job logs in to AWS with OIDC. Where is the AWS access key stored?

options.text: In a repository secret called AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
options.why: That is the old way, and exactly what OIDC removes. A stored key can be printed by any step that runs.

options.text: Nowhere: GitHub signs a token about the job, and AWS trades it for credentials that last minutes
options.why: The role's trust policy checks the token's claims. No long-lived key exists anywhere.

options.text: In Vault, which the job reads first
options.why: Vault is logged in to with the same kind of token. Neither step needs a stored key.

practice.q: zizmor reports dangerous-triggers on a workflow_run workflow that only sends a run ID to a service and never checks out code. What do you do?

options.text: Delete the workflow; zizmor said it is dangerous
options.why: The trigger is risky when a job runs code from a PR with secrets. This job runs none, so the finding does not describe a real risk here.

options.text: Read why the trigger is risky, confirm the job runs no PR code and holds no secrets, and accept the finding
options.why: A checker points at risk; you decide whether it applies. Knowing which findings are real is the skill.

options.text: Switch to pull_request_target so zizmor stops complaining
options.why: pull_request_target runs with the base repo's secrets on PR events, which is the classic way to leak them. It is worse, not better.
